Legal Standards for Qualified Immunity in Excessive Force Claims

In Graham v. Connor, the Supreme Court established the test for determining qualified immunity in excessive force claims. The conduct of law enforcement officers must be judged according to an objective standard without regard to the subjective motivations of the individual officers. The court-approved use of force must be evaluated under the Fourth Amendment's reasonableness standard, considering the need for force, the amount of force used, and the injury inflicted.

Qualified immunity is intended to shield government officials performing discretionary functions, including police officers, from civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known. In Gershkowitz v. Commissioner, 88 T.C. 984, 1987

Gershkowitz v. Commissioner, the tax consequences to an insolvent partner of a partnership's realizing discharge of indebtedness income would become apparent only on the application of such a partnership item to the individual partner's circumstances. However, it is important to note that the partner's distributive share of partnership income and loss was 83 percent, and while there is no snapshot of the partner's financial situation at the time of debt cancellation, the insolvency exception would still apply if the partner was insolvent at the time of debt cancellation.

Discussion

A. Exhaustion of Tribal Remedies

Indian tribes enjoy a quasi-sovereign status under the law. While the federal government may abrogate any aspect of Indian tribal sovereignty, treaties, statutes, regulations, and decisional law provide significant protections to the rights of the tribes to self-government. For example, the Supreme Court has considered the issue of whether the tribes' power to engage in commerce has included an immunity from taxes, and whether the tribal court has jurisdiction to try and punish non-Indians for offenses committed on reservation land.

In Fisher v. District County Court, the Court held that a state court may not exercise jurisdiction over an adoption proceeding in which all parties were tribal members, despite a tribal ordinance purporting to consent to such jurisdiction. The Court explained that the right of the Northern Cheyenne Tribe to govern itself independently of state law has been consistently protected by federal statute.

However, the Supreme Court has also recognized that Indians going beyond reservation boundaries have generally been held subject to nondiscriminatory state law otherwise applicable to all citizens of the State. See Mescalero Apache Tribe v. Jones, 411 U.S. 145, 148
